# Keeping the Maple Street Garden

The garden opens at dawn.

By seven the first volunteers arrive with buckets and gloves, and the beds are already damp from the overnight sprinkler. Ana checks the tomato stakes; Marcus sweeps the paths.

The rhythm is simple, and the garden rewards it. Every bed gets a quarter hour of attention: weeding, watering, and a quiet check for pests. The peas climb their netting in an orderly row, the zucchini sprawls wherever it pleases, and the sunflowers lean toward the fence as though they were listening to the street. It is not a perfect garden, but it is a patient one, and patience, the regulars will tell you, is the whole trick. Even the weeds are part of it: they teach you which mornings are worth the fight.

The work breaks into three tasks:

- Turn the compost every third day, and keep the pile damp.
- Water at the base of each plant, never the leaves.
- Harvest in the morning, before the sun pulls the flavor out.

> “The garden doesn’t need us to hurry,” Ana says. “It needs us to show up.”

On Sunday the gate stays open, and anyone may take a tomato or a sprig of mint. That, too, is part of the rhythm: the garden keeps its promise, and the neighbors keep theirs.
